text: Two of India's favourite first snow treks end at almost exactly the same height, about three thousand eight hundred metres. But on one of them, you climb roughly four hundred metres more to get there. And from the top of the other, you stare at a mountain almost twice as high as where you're standing. Kedarkantha or Brahmatal? By the end of this video, you'll know exactly which one is yours.
This is True Scale. Kedarkantha versus Brahmatal, side by side, in numbers.

Both treks are in Uttarakhand, but in different corners of it. Kedarkantha is in the far west, in Uttarkashi district, near the Himachal border. Its base village is Sankri, about two hundred kilometres from Dehradun. Brahmatal is further east, in Chamoli district. Its base village is Lohajung, the same place where the famous Roopkund trek begins. Two treks, about one hundred and seventy kilometres apart as the crow flies, and two very different personalities.

Kedarkantha is a summit trek. You walk up through pine, oak and maple forest, camp beside a small lake called Juda ka Talab, and then, on the big day, you climb to the top of a mountain. The summit is about three thousand eight hundred metres high, and on a clear morning you see a ring of snow peaks, including Swargarohini, Bandarpunch and Black Peak. It's often described as one of the most popular winter treks in India.

Brahmatal is a ridge and lake trek. You walk through oak and rhododendron forest to Bekaltal, the first lake, then climb onto a long open ridge. The highest point, Brahmatal Top, is about three thousand seven hundred to three thousand eight hundred metres, depending on whose survey you trust. The lake below it is named after Lord Brahma, who is believed to have meditated there. In winter, both lakes can freeze.

So let's put them side by side. Kedarkantha summit, about three thousand eight hundred metres. Brahmatal Top, about three thousand seven hundred and fifty. That's a difference you'd barely notice on the ground. On height alone, this is a tie. But height isn't the whole story.

What matters for your legs is where you start. Sankri sits at about one thousand nine hundred and fifty metres. Lohajung sits higher, at about two thousand three hundred. So on Kedarkantha you gain roughly one thousand eight hundred and fifty metres of height. On Brahmatal, roughly one thousand four hundred. That's about four hundred metres more climbing on Kedarkantha, more than the height of the Eiffel Tower, stacked on top.

Distance and days are close. Both are usually sold as six day trips, with about four days of actual walking. Kedarkantha covers about twenty to twenty three kilometres on foot. Brahmatal covers about twenty two to twenty eight, depending on the route the operator uses. Trek lengths vary a lot between companies, so always check the exact itinerary you're booking.

Getting there is a long drive either way. For Kedarkantha, you drive from Dehradun to Sankri, about two hundred kilometres, which usually takes seven to eleven hours on mountain roads. For Brahmatal, most people come from Kathgodam, the railhead, about two hundred kilometres away, or from Rishikesh, about two hundred and seventy. Plan on ten to twelve hours. Lohajung is the more remote of the two.

Kedarkantha's big moment is summit day. Many groups start in the dark, around four in the morning, to reach the top for sunrise. The final climb is steep and zigzags up the slope, often in snow. The whole day takes about seven to eight hours up and down. It's tough, but standing on a real summit, with mountains on every side, is the reason people come back for this trek again and again.

Brahmatal's big moment is the view. From the ridge, two giants feel close enough to touch. Trishul, about seven thousand one hundred and twenty metres, often described as the first seven thousand metre peak ever climbed, back in nineteen oh seven. And Nanda Ghunti, about six thousand three hundred metres. Put them next to the trek and you see the true scale. Trishul is almost twice as high as the point you're standing on.

The Brahmatal ridge walk, from Tilandi to Jhandi Top and on to Brahmatal Top, is open almost the whole way. You also look across to the meadows of Ali and Bedni Bugyal on the Roopkund route. Instead of one summit push, Brahmatal gives you a whole day of big views, which is why many trekkers call it the more scenic of the two.

Now, the snow. Both are classic winter treks, and both usually have snow from about December into February. Kedarkantha is open around ten months a year, closing for the monsoon. Brahmatal is lovely in autumn for clear views and in early spring, when the rhododendrons bloom and some snow is still left. If snow is the whole point for you, go between late December and February, when your chances are best on either trek.

Then there are the crowds. Kedarkantha's fame is also its problem. One major trekking organisation says the trail from Sankri gets extremely crowded from mid December to mid January, around Christmas and New Year. Some operators now use quieter starting villages to avoid it. Brahmatal is busy in winter too, but it sees fewer people, and it's quietest in autumn, after Diwali.

How hard are they? Both are usually rated easy to moderate, and both are considered suitable for fit beginners. A common fitness target is to be able to cover five kilometres in under forty minutes before you go. The difference is in the shape of the effort. Kedarkantha saves its hardest climb for one long summit day. Brahmatal spreads gentler climbing across several days.

One more thing before you book. In January twenty twenty six, Uttarakhand prepared draft rules for trekking, including registration for operators and certified guides. The draft also asks trekkers to show insurance and a medical certificate. Draft rules can change, so check the latest requirements with your trek operator before you go.

So, which one should you pick? Pick Kedarkantha if you want the feeling of standing on a real summit, if you don't mind crowds, and if you're happy to push hard for one big day. Pick Brahmatal if you want the bigger mountain views, frozen lakes and a long ridge walk, with a little less climbing and a few less people. Either way, it's a superb first taste of Himalayan snow.
Which one would you pick, Kedarkantha or Brahmatal? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe to True Scale for the next Trek versus Trek.
